etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English many, mani, moni, from Old English maniġ, moniġ, maneġ (“many”), from Proto-West Germanic *manag, from Proto-Germanic *managaz (“some, much, many”).

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Genesis 17:4:
quote.text: Thou shalt be a father of many nations.

quote.citation: 1864–65, Charles Dickens, chapter 15, in Our Mutual Friend:
quote.text: I did it in a moment of conceit and folly—one of my many such moments—one of my many such hours—years.

quote.citation: 1909, Archibald Marshall [pseudonym; Arthur Hammond Marshall], chapter III, in The Squire’s Daughter, New York, N.Y.: Dodd, Mead and Company, published 1919, →OCLC:
quote.text: The big houses, and there are a good many of them, lie for the most part in what may be called by courtesy the valleys. You catch a glimpse of them sometimes at a little distance from the [railway] line, which seems to have shown some ingenuity in avoiding them, […].

quote.citation: 2013 July 6, “The rise of smart beta”, in The Economist, volume 408, number 8843, page 68:
quote.text: Investors face a quandary. Cash offers a return of virtually zero in many developed countries; government-bond yields may have risen in recent weeks but they are still unattractive. Equities have suffered two big bear markets since 2000 and are wobbling again. It is hardly surprising that pension funds, insurers and endowments are searching for new sources of return.

definitions.definition: (in combinations such as 'as many', 'so many', 'this many') Used to indicate, demonstrate or compare the number of people or things.
An indefinite large number of people or things.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Luke 1:1:
quote.text: Forasmuch as many have taken in hand to set forth in order a declaration of those things which are most surely believed among us...

quote.citation: 1921, Ben Travers, chapter 4, in A Cuckoo in the Nest, Garden City, N.Y.: Doubleday, Page & Company, published 1925, →OCLC:
quote.text: By some paradoxical evolution rancour and intolerance have been established in the vanguard of primitive Christianity. Mrs. Spoker, in common with many of the stricter disciples of righteousness, was as inclement in demeanour as she was cadaverous in aspect.

definitions.definition: A multitude; a great aggregate; a mass of people; the generality; the common herd.

quote.citation: 2005, Florence Dyer, A Mother's Cry!: Touches the Very Heart of God, page 22:
quote.text: I know that my mother cried a many of times from decisions I made.

quote.citation: 2008 January/February, James Fallows, “The $1.4 Trillion Question”, in The Atlantic Monthly‎[1]:
quote.text: Let’s take these fears about a rich, strong China to their logical extreme. The U.S. and Chinese governments are always disagreeing—about trade, foreign policy, the environment. Someday the disagreement could be severe. Taiwan, Tibet, North Korea, Iran—the possibilities are many, though Taiwan always heads the list.
